paras: The lynching of Curtis B. Hawley and L. V. Grimes was the hanging of two white men by a crowd of citizens at Globe, Arizona Territory, on August 24, 1882, after they confessed to a Wells, Fargo & Co. robbery in which messenger Andy Hall and Dr. W. F. Vail were killed. The crowd spared a third man, Grimes's older brother Cicero, who was later sentenced to 21 years in prison. Wire reports carried the hanging nationally within a day, while Arizona papers printed long accounts of the crowd's orderly proceedings.

On August 20, 1882, robbers fired on the express pack train near Globe and took $5,000 in gold coin; Dr. Vail, riding to his mine, and Hall, who followed the robbers alone, were both shot dead. A Globe dispatch of August 22 predicted that "if caught, the robbers will be lynched," and an early report called the attackers "Three Americans."

Acting on a suspicion from Capt. D. B. Lacy, Deputy U.S. Marshal J. P. Gabriel arrested young Grimes outside Globe, where he confessed and named Hawley, whom Gabriel then arrested in town; Cicero Grimes was jailed on August 23. According to the Florence Enterprise, Gabriel kept the men out of town because he expected a lynching and surrendered them to Gila County officers only on a letter from Attorney McKnabe.

Reports from Globe said the sheriff brought Hawley and Grimes into the jail on the evening of August 23, and resident Samuel W. Bell wrote that more than 200 armed men surrounded it and received the keys. The prisoners were taken to Dr. Stallo's hall, where a "court of inquiry" decided to hang them without delay; Bell described a hearing before a justice of the peace. About thirty citizens then went with the two men to the Pinal mountains foothills, where they showed where the gold was buried.

Meanwhile a young lawyer named Fitch spoke for nearly two hours for Cicero Grimes, followed by O. B. Kennedy and Rev. B. D. Colofee, and officers took him to safety; the Enterprise said Mrs. Vail also asked that he be spared. At a quarter before two in the morning, by a Globe correspondent's account, the church bell tolled and an armed procession led Hawley and Grimes in silence to a sycamore on Main street near Pinal creek, where both were hanged from the same limb. The bodies hung until 8 o'clock, when the coroner held an inquest.

No report of the inquest verdict or of any charge against members of the crowd appears in the coverage. Cicero Grimes was held on $10,000 bail, was found with escape tools in September, pleaded guilty, and on October 2 was sentenced to 21 years as an accessory and taken to Yuma. Gabriel gave his share of the reward for a fence and tombstone at Hall's grave, and quarreled in print with detective John M. Jones over credit for the capture.

The Tucson wire version ran on August 25 and 26 from Washington and St. Paul to Dallas and New York, under heads such as "Murder and Mob Law" and "Lynch Law in Arizona." The St. Paul Daily Globe said the men were "quietly and expeditiously lynched," while the Dallas Daily Herald remarked that lynching "ought not to be indulged in."

Arizona papers praised the officers, dwelt on the crowd's silence and sobriety, and called the hanging "retributive judgment to hardened criminals"; the Enterprise later printed both confessions. Wire copy garbled the names, rendering Grimes as "Gaines," "Grieves" and "Grime."

The Globe correspondent put the hanging at about 1:45 a.m., but the Enterprise, relying on Gabriel, said about ten o'clock Thursday morning. Accounts place the tree near Pinal creek, at the lower end of Main street, or before J. H. Hise's store, and give the crowd as 100 men, more than 200 armed men, or "nearly the adult population of Globe." One version has both men walking without flinching; others say Hawley "died game" while Grimes broke down.

reader.title: Lynching of Curtis B. Hawley and L. V. Grimes
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of Globe citizens took two confessed robbery-murder suspects from officers and the jail and hanged them on a tree in town (A25, A33, A16).

Hawley and L. V. Grimes were hanged by a crowd reported as 100 men to more than 200 armed men after a citizens' 'court of inquiry', with no lawful sentence, in punishment for the robbery and killings they had confessed (A16, A33, A25). The victims were white men, so the episode meets the standard definition but is not anti-Black violence (A26, A22).

Independent local accounts (Enterprise from Gabriel, Citizen special, Chicago Times correspondent, the Bell letter) and the wire all agree that the crowd hanged Hawley and Grimes at Globe and spared Cicero Grimes (A14, A18, A28, A33, A3).

framing.detail: Eastern and Midwestern papers ran short Tucson items under heads such as 'Murder and Mob Law' and 'Lynch Law in Arizona'.
The Globe accounts stressed order and sobriety and closed with 'retributive judgment to hardened criminals'.
The Dallas Daily Herald said lynching 'may sometimes seem good for the health of the country, but it ought not to be indulged in.'
The Enterprise headlined two 'Lynched by the Citizens of Globe, after Confessing' and praised Gabriel's detective work.
